title: Decidability with two parametric clocks and arbitrarily many integer parameters
formal: Is reachability decidable for discrete-time parametric timed automata with at most two parametric clocks and an arbitrary finite number of nonnegative integer parameters?
definitions: An input has finitely many locations, clocks initially zero, parameter symbols, guarded transitions and an initial and target location. A time-elapse step adds the same nonnegative integer to every clock. A transition guard is a conjunction of comparisons \(x\bowtie c\) or \(x\bowtie p\), where c is a nonnegative integer, p a parameter and \(\bowtie\in\{<,\le,=,\ge,>\}\); the transition may reset designated clocks to zero. Other clocks are unchanged. At most two clocks appear in comparisons to parameters; arbitrarily many clocks compared only with constants are allowed. A parameter valuation assigns a nonnegative integer to every parameter once for the entire run. The algorithm must halt on every finite binary encoding and answer whether some valuation permits a finite run to the target. This transition-guard presentation has no extra diagonal or parameter-arithmetic guards.

context_blocks.text: Parametric clocks describe systems whose timing constants are not fixed in advance. Decidability asks whether some assignment of those constants can make a target behavior reachable.

Göller and Hilaire establish EXPSPACE-completeness with two parametric clocks and one parameter in discrete time. They explicitly leave arbitrary numbers of parameters open. Dense-time results and infinite-word acceptance questions use different semantics and cannot be substituted for this finite-reachability target.

why: Resolve a longstanding decidability boundary in timing-parameter synthesis.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
